facts.summary: Montana requires overtime at 1.5x the hourly rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek and has no daily overtime requirement, mirroring the federal standard.
facts.notes: Weekly OT only; no daily OT. Farm workers are exempt and seasonal amusement/recreation students use a 48-hour threshold. Montana does not use a separate higher salary floor for exemptions.

facts.summary: Montana's minimum wage is $10.85 per hour effective January 1, 2026, higher than the federal $7.25, and it is adjusted annually for inflation.
facts.sourceAgency: Montana Department of Labor & Industry, Employment Relations Division
facts.notes: No tip credit, meal credit, or training wage is allowed in Montana. A very small non-FLSA business with gross annual sales of $110,000 or less may pay $4.00/hr. Rate receives a CPI-based cost-of-living adjustment by Sept. 30 each year; verify the current-year figure annually via the official 2026 minimum wage determination letter/poster.

facts.summary: Beyond the federal protected classes, Montana law also prohibits employment discrimination based on marital status, creed, age without a lower-age floor, and (per HB 702) vaccination status.
facts.sourceAgency: Montana Legislature (Montana Code Annotated) / Montana Human Rights Bureau
facts.notes: Section 49-2-303 lists race, creed, religion, color, national origin, age, physical or mental disability, marital status, and sex. Montana's age protection is not limited to workers 40+ (broader than federal ADEA). Vaccination status protection was added by HB 702 (2021), codified at § 49-2-312; see also https://erd.dli.mt.gov/human-rights/human-rights-laws/employment-discrimination/hb-702. Political-ideas protection applies to governmental services, not general private employment.

facts.summary: The Montana Human Rights Act applies to any employer of one or more persons, far lower than the federal 15-employee threshold for Title VII/ADA.
facts.notes: 'Employer' means an employer of one or more persons, excluding certain fraternal, charitable, or religious associations not organized for private profit. Subsection number may shift with recodification; verify current subsection.

facts.value: Wrongful Discharge From Employment Act protects against retaliatory and non-good-cause discharge
facts.summary: Montana is not a pure at-will state: after an employee completes the probationary period, discharge is wrongful if it was retaliation for refusing to violate or for reporting a violation of public policy, was not for good cause, or violated the employer's written personnel policy.
facts.notes: Montana is the only state with a general good-cause discharge statute (the WDEA). Default probationary period is 12 months absent a specified period. During probation employment remains at will.

facts.value: 180 days to file; recover up to 2 years (3 years for repeated violations)
facts.summary: An employee must file a wage claim within 180 days of the default or delay in payment and may recover wages and penalties for the prior 2 years (3 years for repeated violations).
facts.notes: 180-day filing deadline for the administrative complaint; the 2-/3-year window governs the lookback period for recoverable wages and penalties.

facts.summary: A discrimination complaint must be filed with the Montana Human Rights Bureau within 180 days after the alleged discriminatory act occurred or was discovered.
facts.sourceAgency: Montana Legislature (Montana Code Annotated) / Montana Human Rights Bureau
facts.notes: Extension available where a grievance procedure under a CBA/contract/policy is used: up to 300 days if the grievance procedure extends beyond 120 days. This state deadline is shorter than the EEOC's 300-day deferral-state deadline; claimants should watch both.

facts.value: Involuntary: immediately (or per written policy, next payday or within 15 days, whichever is first); Voluntary: next payday or within 15 days, whichever is first
facts.summary: On involuntary separation, final wages are due immediately unless a written personnel policy extends payment to the next payday or within 15 days; employees who quit are paid on the next regular payday or within 15 days, whichever comes first.
facts.notes: Late-payment penalties are set by § 39-3-206 (penalty up to 110% of wages due). Section URL constructed from the MCA Part 2 index for § 39-3-205; verify the exact section page.
